strengths: Very broad empirical evaluation: 29 datasets across 8 tasks (fine-grained understanding, bbox classification, OVD, retrieval, classification, segmentation, LMM integration), covering both English and Chinese, with consistent state-of-the-art results and sensible baselines (SigLIP 2, Meta CLIP 2, FG-CLIP, Chinese-CLIP, R2D2).

The Textual Intra-modal Contrastive (TIC) loss is a simple but well-motivated idea for sharpening the text encoder's representation space, and the ablation (Table 7) shows both TIC and CMR contribute meaningfully, especially jointly (COCO Top-1 dropping from 74.9 to 62.7 when both are removed).

Introduction of a new Chinese fine-grained benchmark suite (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) addresses a genuine gap — existing Chinese benchmarks are mostly short-caption retrieval — and the construction pipeline is described in reasonable detail, with examples provided in the appendix.

Comprehensive implementation details (optimizer, batch sizes, resolution strategy, training hardware) and appendix material on OVD/segmentation setups improve reproducibility of the released components; the paper promises release of model, code, and benchmark.
The paper honestly notes the model achieves strong results without sacrificing standard zero-shot classification performance (Table 3), addressing a common regression in fine-grained CLIP variants.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is largely an assembly of existing components (SigLIP 2 architecture and sigmoid loss, FineHARD hard negatives and region-text learning from FG-CLIP, CMR loss from Zhang et al. 2024b, MAP head, RoIAlign). The TIC loss is a straightforward intra-modal contrastive with filtered top-k hard negatives; no theoretical analysis or deeper insight is offered about why or when it works.

Reproducibility gaps from undisclosed data: the largest Chinese data sources (500M image-text pairs and 12M region-text pairs, i.e., the bulk of Chinese training data) are 'in-house' and presumably not released. The claimed advantage over Chinese-CLIP/R2D2/Meta CLIP 2 may stem substantially from proprietary data rather than the method, and the paper does not attempt to disentangle data quantity from method contributions (no controlled ablation on data scale or composition).

Potential train-test contamination in the proposed benchmark: BoxClass-CN is constructed from the LAION-2B corpus, while the model itself is trained on 'LAION-2B-enhanced' (1.6B pairs). The paper does not state whether deduplication was performed between training images and the 24,221 benchmark images, which is essential given FG-CLIP 2 is also used to filter the benchmark's region-text pairs (similarity > 0.15 computed by FG-CLIP), creating a self-reinforcing bias.

Circularity/bias in Chinese long-caption benchmarks: LIT-CN, DCI-CN, and DOCCI-CN captions are generated or translated by Qwen2.5-VL, and the evaluating models' captions during training were also LMM-generated. Models trained with similar caption-generation pipelines may be systematically favored; no analysis of this bias (e.g., human-verified subset performance) is provided.

Ablations are narrow: only LCMR and TIC are ablated. There is no ablation of the two-stage schedule, the long/short dual-caption strategy, region-text objectives (LFGV/LFGT), loss weights (chosen without justification), data-adaptive resolution vs. SigLIP 2's native aspect-ratio sampling, or text length 196.

Presentation quality issues: numerous typos ('empoly', 'a water fall that are used as a water source' in Figure 1, 'Chinese' rendered inconsistently), Table 1's table note ordering, and some terse descriptions (e.g., the 'additional self-attention module' for dense embeddings is not specified in enough detail to reimplement).

Ethics and limitations treatment is thin: web-scraped data (LAION, Wukong, Zero, in-house) carries known content and privacy concerns; no data governance, licensing, or bias discussion for the Chinese in-house corpus; the limitations paragraph is essentially a restatement of the conclusion with a single sentence on future work rather than a genuine discussion of e.g. contamination or benchmark validity risks.

strengths: Extensive and broad empirical evaluation: results across 29 datasets and 8 tasks spanning fine-grained understanding, bounding box classification, open-vocabulary detection, retrieval (short and long caption), zero-shot classification, open-vocabulary segmentation, and LMM integration, with consistent gains at three model scales (Base, Large, So400M).

A genuinely useful contribution to an underserved area: the Chinese benchmark suite (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) addresses a real gap, as existing Chinese benchmarks focus on short-caption retrieval, and region-level Chinese evaluation was largely absent.
Comprehensive ablation (Table 7) isolating the two proposed losses, showing complementary effects (COCO Top-1 drops from 74.9 to 62.7 when both CMR and TIC are removed).

Strong engineering and reproducibility intentions: the model, code, and benchmark are promised for release, implementation details (hardware, batch sizes, optimizer settings, fusion strategy in Appendix B) are reported in unusual depth, and the paper honestly notes reliance on prior components.

Fair comparison practice in places: models are compared at matched backbone scales, and the paper acknowledges that gains on ImageNet-1K/v2 are only competitive with SigLIP 2 rather than superior, suggesting a balanced representation.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the framework is assembled almost entirely from existing pieces — SigLIP 2 architecture and sigmoid loss, the FineHARD hard-negative data and region-text training from FG-CLIP, the CMR loss from Zhang et al. (2024b), and MAP pooling from LiT. The only newly proposed component, the TIC loss (Eq. 4), is a small variant of the intra-modal contrastive loss (CAO) from that same prior work, with a similarity filter and top-K hard negative selection.

Potential evaluation circularity in the new Chinese benchmarks, which are the paper's headline contribution: BoxClass-CN is constructed by retaining boxes with region-text similarity above 0.15 computed using FG-CLIP (the authors' own prior model), which plausibly favors the FG-CLIP lineage (FG-CLIP and FG-CLIP 2) at evaluation time. LIT-CN captions are generated by Qwen2.5-VL in a style similar to the LMM-generated long captions used in FG-CLIP 2's training data, so the model may be advantaged by stylistic matching rather than genuinely better Chinese understanding.

The Chinese training data includes a 500M-pair in-house dataset and a 12M-image in-house region-text dataset that cannot be released or independently audited, making exact reproduction impossible and weakening comparability with baselines (e.g., Chinese-CLIP, R2D2) that trained on substantially less data. The claimed advantage over Meta CLIP 2 partly conflates data scale/specialization with the training recipe.

No contamination analysis: Chinese benchmarks are derived via LMM translation/recaptioning of DCI and DOCCI and from LAION-2B images that overlap the training corpus; the paper does not check for train-test leakage or caption overlap.

Weak experimental support for some design claims: the data-adaptive resolution strategy and the choice of the five loss weights (λ1..λ5) are asserted as 'chosen to ensure stable and effective' but never ablated; ablations cover only the two ranking/contrastive losses and only at one scale. The global-threshold synchronization in Eq. 3 is not compared against a simple fixed margin or local batch statistic.

Some baselines are disadvantaged: SigLIP 2 is English-centric yet included in Chinese tables, and the prose leans on these large gaps (e.g., 16.3 vs. 87.6 R@1 on LIT-CN) as evidence of superiority when a bilingual baseline like Meta CLIP 2 narrows them considerably (77.2).

Presentation issues: 'Code&Model&Dataset:' appears as an empty placeholder on page 1; typos ('We empoly', 'a artificial flower'); Table C provides only qualitative LIT-CN examples, and no human evaluation of the machine-translated DCI-CN/DOCCI-CN captions beyond 'validated by native speakers' with no protocol detail.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper reports results on 29 datasets across 8 vision-language tasks (fine-grained understanding, bbox classification, OVD, long/short retrieval, zero-shot classification, segmentation, LMM benchmarks) at three model scales, which is unusually broad for this line of work and includes strong baselines such as SigLIP 2, MetaCLIP 2, FG-CLIP, and FineCLIP.

The new Chinese benchmark suite (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN long-caption retrieval and BoxClass-CN region classification) fills a genuine gap, since existing Chinese benchmarks (COCO-CN, Flickr30k-CNA) only cover short-caption retrieval; the construction pipeline and full category schema are documented in the appendix.

The proposed Textual Intra-modal Contrastive (TIC) loss is a reasonable, well-motivated idea for sharpening the text space against semantically similar region descriptions, and the ablation (Table 7) shows a meaningful 4.8-point COCO Top-1 drop when it is removed, with additional complementary gains from the CMR loss.

The bilingual framing is significant: FG-CLIP 2 outperforms MetaCLIP 2 (ViT-H/14, 1.8B params) on Chinese retrieval with a smaller ViT-L/16 backbone, and demonstrates that fine-grained and multilingual objectives can be combined without sacrificing ImageNet classification, addressing a real weakness of prior Chinese CLIP models.
The paper releases model, code, and benchmark, and includes an implementation appendix with training configuration details that support reproducibility of the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the overall recipe is largely an assembly of existing techniques — region-text matching and FineHARD hard negatives come from FG-CLIP, the CMR loss is adopted from Zhang et al. (2024b), the sigmoid loss and MAP head from SigLIP/SigLIP 2, RoIAlign from Mask R-CNN — so the conceptual contribution beyond FG-CLIP is the TIC loss plus a data curation effort, which is more of a systems/engineering contribution.

Potential circularity in the BoxClass-CN benchmark: region-text pairs are filtered using FG-CLIP similarity scores (region-text similarity above 0.15 computed by FG-CLIP), and categories were refined via a pipeline involving FG-CLIP-related components. This means the proposed benchmark may be systematically biased in favor of FG-CLIP-family models, undermining the claim that FG-CLIP 2's large gains on BoxClass-CN (60.7 vs. SigLIP 2's 57.9) reflect genuine fine-grained capability rather than a construction artifact.

Evaluation data contamination risk: LIT-CN, DCI-CN, and DOCCI-CN captions are generated by Qwen2.5-VL, and the training data relies heavily on LMM-generated long captions. Models trained on LMM-recaptioned data are plausibly favored on LMM-generated evaluation sets; no analysis (e.g., human-annotated subsets or evaluation on natively authored Chinese captions) is provided to rule this out.

Reproducibility concerns: the largest Chinese data sources (500M-pair in-house image-text data and 12M-image in-house region-text data) cannot be released, so the exact training mixture is not fully reproducible; the 'Code&Model&Dataset:' link on the title page is an unfilled placeholder, so the release status cannot be verified from the manuscript.

Ablation coverage is narrow: Table 7 only ablates the CMR and TIC losses on a subset of tasks. There is no ablation of the two-stage curriculum, the dual (short+long) caption strategy, the data-adaptive resolution scheme, loss weights, or the contribution of Chinese vs. English data to bilingual performance, so the attribution of gains to specific design choices is incomplete.

The paper contains signs of a not-fully-polished manuscript: an unfinished link placeholder, typos ('We empoly'), and the ablation table shows the 'Trivial' FG-OVD subset is actually higher without the proposed losses (93.5 vs. 92.0), which is not discussed.

Comparison fairness is not fully controlled: FG-CLIP 2 is trained on a much larger Chinese corpus (850M pairs including proprietary data) than Chinese-CLIP or R2D2, so the strong Chinese results partly reflect data scale; no compute- or data-matched comparison isolates the benefit of the training objectives.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: results across 29 datasets and 8 task families (fine-grained understanding, bounding-box classification, OVD, retrieval in both languages, zero-shot classification, segmentation, and LLaVA-style LMM integration), with strong, consistent gains over well-chosen baselines including MetaCLIP 2 despite a smaller backbone.

Valuable community resources: a newly released 12M Chinese region-text dataset (FineRegion-CN), four new Chinese evaluation benchmarks (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN), plus model and code releases — addressing a genuine gap in non-English fine-grained evaluation.

Careful ablation work: loss-weight sweeps (Appendix F), ablations of the proposed CMR and TIC objectives (Table 8), a bilingual data-composition ablation (Table C), and — notably — a controlled comparison with re-trained SigLIP 2 and Chinese-CLIP baselines on identical Stage II data (Table D), which supports that architectural/objective choices, not just data scale, drive the gains.
Embedding visualizations (Appendices G, H, Tables E.1/E.2) give qualitative evidence that the TIC loss improves separation of semantically similar captions in both languages.

Clear presentation: the two-stage training framework, data pipeline, and benchmark construction procedures are described with enough detail (hyperparameters, dataset statistics, full category lists) to follow and largely reproduce the released components.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the framework is largely an assembly of existing techniques (SigLIP 2 backbone and sigmoid loss, RoIAlign-based region alignment following FG-CLIP, FineHARD-style hard negatives, CMR loss from Zhang et al. 2024b). The only genuinely new objective, the TIC loss, is a simple intra-modal contrastive over similarity-filtered hard negatives (Eq. 1), and its ablation shows modest deltas on FG-OVD Hard (52.3→51.6).

Potential circularity in the newly proposed benchmarks: LIT-CN captions are generated by Qwen2.5-VL, the same LMM-family recaptioning strategy used to build the training data, and BoxClass-CN boxes/captions are filtered using FG-CLIP similarity scores — i.e., the predecessor of the evaluated model. This risks systematically favoring FG-CLIP 2 on the new Chinese long-caption retrieval and region-classification benchmarks (e.g., the very large gaps over SigLIP 2 in Table 5), and this bias is not analyzed or mitigated.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the 500M-pair Chinese 'in-house dataset' is not released and its provenance/curation is not described, so full Stage I training cannot be reproduced; the paper also ships with blank Homepage/Code/Model links at submission time.

The ablation of training objectives (Table 8) only removes LCMR and LTIC; the individual contributions of LFGV and LFGT are never isolated, so the marginal value of each component in the composite objective is not fully established.

Claims of bilingual capability rest on a two-language setting; no results on other languages are given, so the generalization of the framework beyond English–Chinese remains untested, and the limitations section does not discuss data-quality risks of LMM-generated captions (hallucinations, translation errors) beyond noting native-speaker validation for only the CN benchmark translations.

Minor presentation issues: Table E.1/E.2 similarity matrices are hard to read at print size; Figure 1 is dense; and several implementation details (e.g., the exact LMM used for LAION long-caption augmentation) are unspecified.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the model is assessed on 29 datasets across 8 task families (fine-grained understanding, bounding box classification, open-vocabulary detection, retrieval in both languages, zero-shot classification, dense prediction, and LMM integration), with results at three backbone scales, which is well above the norm for CLIP-style papers.

A genuine resource contribution: the 12M-image FineRegion-CN Chinese region-text dataset and a new Chinese evaluation suite (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) address a real gap, as Chinese evaluation is currently limited to short-caption retrieval (COCO-CN, Flickr-CNA).

The paper includes controlled experiments that isolate confounds: Table C varies bilingual vs. English-only Stage II data, and Appendix E re-trains SigLIP 2 and Chinese-CLIP on identical Stage II data, supporting the claim that the objectives (not just data) drive gains.

The TIC loss is supported by ablations (Table 8: 4.8-point COCO drop when removed) and qualitative similarity-matrix visualizations (Tables E.1/E.2) showing improved separation of near-duplicate captions in both languages.

Results are strong where it matters for the claims: FG-CLIP 2 beats MetaCLIP 2 (ViT-H/14) on bilingual retrieval with a smaller ViT-L/16 backbone, and improves OVD and segmentation when plugged into LLMDet and Cat-Seg.
The authors commit to releasing model, code, training data, and benchmarks, which supports reproducibility and community reuse.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the system is largely an assembly of existing components — SigLIP 2 backbone, FG-CLIP's region-text and hard-negative losses, the CMR loss from Zhang et al. (2024b), and RoIAlign. The proposed TIC loss is essentially an intra-modal contrastive term (closely related to the intra-modal part of Zhang et al., 2024b), so the scientific delta over FG-CLIP + SigLIP 2 is modest.

Potential circularity in the newly proposed benchmarks: BoxClass-CN is filtered using FG-CLIP similarity scores, and LIT-CN/DCI-CN captions are generated by Qwen2.5-VL, the same LMM-caption style used to construct the training data. FG-CLIP 2, trained on LMM-generated long captions, may have a systematic advantage on these benchmarks; results on these self-built benchmarks should be interpreted with caution and independently verified.

The zero-shot classification claim is overstated: on ImageNet-1K/IN-v2, FG-CLIP 2 actually underperforms SigLIP 2 (79.5 vs 81.2 at ViT-B/16; 83.0 vs 83.1 at ViT-L/16). Describing this as 'competitive' masks a regression on the standard recognition axis, and the paper does not analyze the trade-off.

Reproducibility gaps: the 500M-pair 'in-house' Chinese dataset is not characterized (sources, filtering, licensing), Stage I training details (duration, tokens seen, data processing) are thin, and the Homepage/Code/Model links in the submission are blank. Compute cost is also unreported, making it hard to judge the efficiency claims relative to MetaCLIP 2.

Ablations are only performed at ViT-B/16; it is unclear whether the auxiliary losses (TIC, CMR) and their fixed weights (chosen via a sequential tuning procedure that admits suboptimality) transfer across scales.

Some inconsistencies weaken confidence: Table C shows bilingual data yields only marginal English improvements (e.g., DCI 64.4→64.5), which sits awkwardly with the strong 'mutually promoting effect' claim; and the CMR margin-sync mechanism is adopted without analysis of its behavior at scale.

The limitations discussion is thin: no discussion of multilingual generalization beyond Chinese/English, of the self-constructed-benchmark risk, or of the potential for LMM-generated caption noise in training data.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-controlled evaluation: results span 29 datasets across 8 tasks (fine-grained understanding, bounding box classification, OVD, retrieval, zero-shot classification, segmentation, and LMM integration), with consistent SOTA or competitive results at multiple backbone scales (ViT-B/L/So).

The comparison against MetaCLIP 2 is compelling: FG-CLIP 2 with a smaller ViT-So/ViT-L backbone outperforms the 1.8B-parameter ViT-H multilingual SOTA on both English and Chinese tasks, supporting the claim that the training paradigm rather than scale drives the gains.

Valuable community resources: a new 12M-image Chinese region-text dataset (FineRegion-CN), a new Chinese benchmark suite (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN), and stated public release of model, code, and data address a genuine gap in non-English fine-grained evaluation.

Ablations are unusually thorough for this paper class: loss-component ablations (Table 8), bilingual vs. English-only data ablation (Table C), hyperparameter sweeps (Figure B), and — importantly — retrained-baseline comparisons under identical Stage II data (Table D) that isolate the contribution of the architecture/objectives from the data.

The proposed TIC loss is simple, well-motivated (intra-modal hard negatives sharpen the text space for grounding), and supported by both quantitative ablations (4.8-point COCO drop when removed) and qualitative embedding visualizations (Appendix H/E.1-E.2).
The cross-modal rank loss with globally synchronized margins (Eq. 3) is a sensible engineering contribution for distributed training stability.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the paper is primarily a strong engineering/data contribution building directly on FG-CLIP. The FGT objective and hard negatives come from FG-CLIP/FineHARD, the CMR loss is adopted from Zhang et al. (2024b), and TIC is a straightforward intra-modal contrastive variant. This is acceptable for a systems paper but the conceptual advance over FG-CLIP is modest.

Potential circularity in the proposed Chinese benchmarks: LIT-CN captions are generated by Qwen2.5-VL, and FG-CLIP 2's training data heavily uses LMM-generated long captions (LAION-2B-enhanced, FineRegion-CN pipeline). Models trained on stylistically similar LMM captions (i.e., FG-CLIP 2 itself) may be systematically favored over models trained on human captions; the paper does not analyze or acknowledge this bias, e.g., via a human-written Chinese caption subset. Similarly, BoxClass-CN categories were filtered using FG-CLIP similarity, and only SigLIP 2/MetaCLIP 2 baselines are reported on it.

Reproducibility gaps: a 500M-pair in-house Chinese dataset is used but not (apparently) released; benchmark construction details such as the LIT-CN 'curated web images' source and translation QC protocol are only sketched; implementation details like training epochs and sequence handling are thin. The claimed release of model/code/benchmark partially mitigates this but cannot be verified from the manuscript.

Some evaluation asymmetries: SigLIP 2 is not bilingual, so its near-zero Chinese retrieval scores (Table 5) are expected and add little; the OVD results use a fusion/recalibration protocol whose gains over the base detector alone are not decomposed. Table 8's ablation shows FG-OVD 'Trivial' slightly improving when LCMR is removed, which is unexplained.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., 'empoly', incomplete homepage/code links in the manuscript, Figure B's axes merely summarize averages across heterogeneous tasks), and the limitations section is brief, not discussing benchmark bias, data licensing/copyright of LAION/Wukong/Zero-derived data, or the societal implications of web-scale training data beyond a boilerplate impact statement.

The claim of 'none explicitly optimize both [fine-grained and multilingual] in a unified framework' overlooks some multilingual fine-grained efforts (e.g., recent multilingual SigLIP-style models with localization objectives), and the paper limits itself to two languages where a broader multilingual treatment would strengthen generality.
